A jowl is the soft, fleshy part of your lower cheek and jaw area — the thick, meaty part of your face near the sides of your chin. Think of it as the lower, outer region of your face where your cheek meets your jaw.

To picture it: if you were to cup your hand around the bottom of someone's face — below the cheekbone, above the neck, on either side of the chin — you'd be covering their jowls.
The Key Detail: Heaviness and Sagging

The word jowl almost always carries a sense of weight and fleshiness. It's not typically used to describe a slim, tight face. Instead, it describes tissue that is:

  • Thick and full, or
  • Loose and drooping downward, especially with age or weight gain

This is why you'll most often hear the word in its plural form — jowls — describing both sides of the lower face together. A common image is an older person whose skin has lost its firmness, causing the lower cheeks to droop or sag slightly below the jawline. Writers and speakers use "jowls" to paint a picture of this heaviness. For example:

"His jowls wobbled as he shook his head."
"She had the heavy jowls of someone well into their seventies."

Even when the skin isn't fully sagging, "jowls" still implies fullness and weight in that part of the face.

Jowl is also used for animals, particularly dogs and pigs, to mean the same region — the cheek and lower jaw area.

Some dog breeds are famous for their jowls. A Basset Hound or Bloodhound, for instance, has dramatically loose, droopy skin hanging from the sides of their lower face — those folds of loose skin are their jowls. The word fits animals just as naturally as it fits humans.

In cooking and butchery, jowl refers to the cheek meat of a pig, cut from the jaw and lower face area of the animal. You'll see it written as pork jowl or hog jowl. It's a fatty, rich cut of meat that is often smoked or cured, similar to bacon. In the American South, eating hog jowls (especially on New Year's Day) is a longstanding tradition believed to bring good luck.

So in a food context, jowl simply refers to that same physical region of an animal — now as a cut of meat.
A Very Common Phrase: "Cheek by Jowl"

You will encounter jowl in one very popular idiom:

Cheek by jowl

This phrase means very close together, side by side, in tight proximity — almost uncomfortably so. The phrase paints a picture of two people standing so close that their cheeks and jowls are nearly touching. For example:

"The apartments were built cheek by jowl, with barely any space between them."
"Hundreds of protesters stood cheek by jowl in the narrow street."

You'll hear this phrase used for both people and objects. It always signals extreme closeness or crowding.

ContextWhat it means

Jowl always refers to the same physical place: the fleshy, lower cheek and jaw region. Whether you're describing a person's aging face, a dog's droopy skin folds, a cut of pig meat, or using the idiom "cheek by jowl," the word is anchored to that one location on the body — just viewed through different lenses.

The emotional weight of the word, when used about people, is usually one of age, heaviness, or physical fullness — never delicate or slim. Keep that image in mind and you'll always understand jowl in any sentence you meet it.
